text: Greenland is about two thirds the size of India. India is home to more than a billion people. Greenland? Fifty six thousand seven hundred and forty. That's the whole country. You could fit every single person in Greenland inside Ahmedabad's Narendra Modi Stadium, and still have more than half the seats left empty. So why does almost nobody live on the biggest island on Earth?
This is True Scale. Why nobody lives in Greenland.

And right now, Greenland is in the news. On the third of November, its parliament approved a security deal with the United States and Denmark. Sixteen votes for, none against, and seven abstentions. The deal lets the United States modernise and expand its activities at Pituffik Space Base, in the far northwest. Denmark's parliament is due to debate it later this month. To understand why the world suddenly cares so much about such an empty place, we need to see it at its true scale.

On most wall maps, Greenland looks enormous, because the Mercator projection stretches everything near the poles. On a fair map, it shrinks. Its real area is about two point one seven million square kilometres. India is about three point two nine million. So Greenland really is huge, roughly two thirds of India, but spread across all that space are fewer than sixty thousand people. That works out to about one person for every thirty eight square kilometres.

Reason number one is the biggest. About eighty percent of Greenland is buried under a single sheet of ice. The Greenland ice sheet covers roughly one point seven million square kilometres. Take that away, and the ice-free land is only a rim around the edge, roughly four hundred and fifty thousand square kilometres in total, much of it bare rock and mountains.

And this ice is not a thin crust. At its thickest point, it's more than three kilometres deep. Greenland's highest mountain, Gunnbjorn Fjeld, is about three thousand six hundred and ninety four metres tall. So in the middle of the island, the ice alone is almost as tall as the country's highest peak. There are no towns up there. There is no soil to farm and nothing to build on, just ice in every direction.

In total, the ice sheet holds about two point nine million cubic kilometres of ice. If all of it melted, global sea level would rise by about seven point four metres. That's why scientists watch Greenland so closely. Antarctica's ice sheet is far bigger, enough for about fifty eight metres, but Greenland's alone could reshape coastlines around the world.

Reason number two is the cold. Even the capital, Nuuk, sits on the milder southwest coast, and its warmest month, July, averages only about seven degrees Celsius. The average high in July is around ten and a half degrees. In February, the average is minus eight. And that's the mild part of the country. Further north, and on the ice, it's far colder.

So people live where the ice ends and the sea begins. Greenland's coastline is about forty four thousand kilometres long, and almost every town clings to it. Nuuk is the biggest by far, with about twenty thousand three hundred people. That's more than a third of the entire population in a single town. Around eighty nine percent of Greenlanders live in towns, and the rest in small settlements along the coast.

Reason number three: there are no roads between towns. Not one road connects two towns in Greenland. To travel from one to another, you fly, take a boat, or, for nearby places, go by dog sled. Air Greenland's planes carry up to thirty seven passengers, and smaller settlements without a runway are served by helicopter. A coastal passenger ship runs between Qaqortoq and Ilulissat, but only from April to December. Imagine every trip to the next town being a flight.

But Greenland was never truly empty. People have lived here for thousands of years. The first known groups, called Independence One and Saqqaq, arrived around four and a half thousand years ago. Later came the Dorset people. Then, around the year eleven hundred, the Thule people arrived, the ancestors of today's Greenlandic Inuit. They learned to live with the ice and the sea, and their descendants still make up most of the population.

In the late nine hundreds, Norse settlers arrived from Iceland, led by Erik the Red, who, according to the old sagas, gave the island its hopeful name. They lived in the southwest for more than four hundred years. But their settlements declined in the fourteen hundreds and were abandoned. The Inuit stayed. In seventeen twenty one, the missionary Hans Egede arrived, and the Danish colonial era began.

Greenland became part of the Kingdom of Denmark in nineteen fifty three. It gained home rule in nineteen seventy nine, and wider self government in two thousand and nine. Today Greenlanders run most of their own affairs, but Denmark still handles foreign affairs and security. Nearly nine in ten people living there were born in Greenland.

Reason number four is the economy. With no roads between towns, almost everything moves by ship or plane. Fishing produces about ninety percent of Greenland's exports. And Denmark sends an annual block grant, about four point one billion Danish kroner in twenty twenty three, which makes up roughly half of the Greenland government's revenue. A small population, a huge area and very few roads make every hospital, school and power line harder to pay for.

So why does such an empty island matter so much? Location. Greenland sits between North America and Europe, at the edge of the Arctic. The United States already operates Pituffik Space Base there. Greenland's natural resources include zinc, gold, uranium and rare earth minerals. And as the Arctic warms, many expect its sea routes and resources to become easier to reach. An island that almost nobody lives on is suddenly one that everybody wants a say in.

So, why does nobody live in Greenland? Four reasons. Four fifths of it is buried under ice up to three kilometres thick. Even the ice-free rim is cold, with the capital's warmest month averaging about seven degrees. There are no roads between towns, so every journey is a flight or a voyage. And a tiny population has to pay for services spread across an area two thirds the size of India.

Would you live in Greenland for a year, if someone paid your rent? Tell me in the comments. And if you liked seeing the world at its true scale, subscribe to True Scale. There's a lot more of the map to fix.
